content: The Guideline Review Committee (GRC) approved the technical statement summarizing the conclusions and updated recommendations from the meeting held on February 15, 2012. This approval was a critical step in the process of developing the fifth edition of the Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (MEC). Both the planning and finalization of the document were endorsed by the GRC. The development of the fifth edition of the MEC involved several key groups, including the WHO Secretariat, an Evidence Secretariat with a GRADE methodologist, a Guideline Steering Group (GSG), and a Guideline Development Group (GDG). The GDG, previously known as the Expert Working Group for earlier MEC editions, included the GSG, which has served as an external advisory group to WHO on family planning guidelines since 2003. This structure ensured compliance with WHO requirements for guideline development and allowed input from a broader advisory group. To prioritize topics for the revision process, the first GDG meeting was held on May 14–15, 2013, in Ferney-Voltaire, France. Before this meeting, the Continuous Identification of Research Evidence (CIRE) system was used to identify recommendations from the fourth edition of the MEC for which new evidence was available. The WHO Secretariat also consulted a wide range of stakeholders with expertise in family planning, including representatives from implementing agencies, professional societies, WHO regional and country offices, and Ministries of Health in Member States. These stakeholders were invited to complete a 24-question anonymous electronic survey, available in English, French, and Spanish, between March 2 and May 2, 2013. Respondents ranked the importance of various outcomes related to priority topics, suggested additional outcomes and clinical questions, and provided feedback on the format of the guidance. Over 250 completed surveys were submitted, and the results were presented to the GDG during the meeting to inform the prioritization process. During the meeting, the WHO Secretariat presented summaries of new evidence to the GDG to determine whether existing recommendations remained consistent or had become inconsistent with the updated evidence. Recommendations deemed potentially inconsistent with the new evidence were selected for further discussion at a larger meeting in March 2014. Recommendations considered consistent with the updated evidence or for which no new evidence was identified through CIRE were determined by the GDG to require no further review during the revision process. The GDG also reviewed whether WHO should include new conditions, contraceptive methods, or formulations based on their global relevance and availability in multiple countries. Additionally, the group examined two interim guidance documents released since the fourth edition and addressed recommendations classified as category 2/3 in the fourth edition, which had been noted as potentially confusing to users. Topics were prioritized for review at the second GDG meeting in March 2014 based on criteria such as controversy, new evidence, interim guidance, newly introduced contraceptive methods, or lack of clarity in existing recommendations. Systematic reviews were conducted to assess the safety risks of using specific contraceptive methods among women with particular medical conditions or characteristics. These reviews were informed by PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) questions, which guided the focus on relevant studies. The reviews assessed both direct and indirect evidence and were peer-reviewed by selected GDG members. GRADE evidence profiles were prepared to evaluate the quality of the summarized evidence and included estimates of effect for each clinical outcome assessed. Printed copies of these profiles were provided to GDG members during the March 2014 meeting, and the systematic reviews served as the basis for the GDG's deliberations. The GDG meetings held on March 9–12 and September 24–25, 2014, reviewed evidence for priority topics and revised specific recommendations in the MEC where appropriate. Members of the GDG and the External Peer Review Group submitted Declaration of Interest forms to the WHO Secretariat. While most declarations revealed no conflicts of interest, two members (Dr. Glasier and Dr. Sitruk-Ware) disclosed academic conflicts of interest that precluded their participation in deliberations related to specific topics (ulipristal acetate and the progesterone-releasing vaginal ring, respectively). The GDG considered the overall quality of safety evidence using the GRADE approach, focusing on the strength and consistency of the data. In most cases, the quality of evidence was low or very low and primarily addressed potential harms related to contraceptive use. The GDG used a 1–4 scale to categorize medical eligibility for contraceptive use, reflecting eligibility rather than defining recommendations as strong or weak per GRADE methodology. Through consensus, the GDG arrived at new and revised recommendations while reaffirming the majority of existing recommendations. The final version of the MEC fifth edition was approved by the GRC on March 18, 2015. Dissemination of the recommendations included a global live Facebook chat on June 1, 2015, and collaboration with various organizations and civil society groups engaged in sexual and reproductive health projects.
